## Local modifications

**None.** The bytes are unmodified, and that is proven rather than recorded.

`GIT-ANCHOR.json` stores the raw git objects for the path from the pinned commit to each blob:
the commit object, the root tree, `qa`, `fixtures`, and each fixture directory.
`tests/test_ats_semantic_replay.py` re-hashes every stored object, walks
commit → root → qa → fixtures → directory → blob, and compares the resulting blob id to the
bytes on disk. Because changing a blob changes its id, which changes the tree naming it, which
changes the tree above it, which changes the commit — and the commit id is the constant the
test starts from — the chain cannot be forged offline. Editing a vendored file and updating
the digests beside it does not keep the test green; that was checked by doing it.

`SHA256SUMS.json` keeps SHA-256 digests as a convenience. It is not the anchor, because a
manifest stored next to the files it describes can only compare the vendoring to itself.

## Not copied

The upstream worker, recorder, compiler, QA process, scenarios, private recordings, screenshots,
DOM captures, documentation, and every other fixture. Nothing here is upstream executable code.

## What these files are, and are not

They are **compiled semantic models**: field `kind`, ARIA `role`, label, `choices`, and
`required`, with the original recording reduced upstream to a `sourceRecordingSha256` that is
not published. Upstream states its recorded lanes are closed replay fixtures and that its
guided flows for other platforms are unverified and may drift.

So they are evidence that **a field combination came from a real recording**. They are

- **not** captured DOM,
- **not** CSS selectors,
- **not** screenshots,
- **not** current live-site acceptance evidence,
- **not** permission to access any site.

A passing local replay therefore says the field combination is handled. It says nothing about
whether current Lever, Greenhouse, or Ashby DOM can be filled. Each production adapter still
requires its own supervised live acceptance test, per `docs/adr-fill-only-browser-worker.md`.

## Rendering

The local HTML is generated by Jobloom-owned code in
`skills/jobloom/scripts/semantic_replay.py` from these semantic models. No upstream markup is
reproduced, because none was published.

The replay also serves `/lever/split/0` and `/lever/split/1`. Those are **four** of the Lever
fixture's twenty-seven recorded controls, re-paginated across two pages so a flow with two
action packages has two pages of fields to work with. It is not a two-page replay of the Lever
form, and the pagination is not upstream's — every reviewed fixture puts all its controls on
one step with the final action alone on the next.

Control labels are rendered **as recorded**, not paraphrased, because a paraphrase would test
a form no employer ships. Recorded wording is not synthetic wording, and the page says so; no
banner makes it otherwise.

Option values are distinct from labels, as on a real control. The renderer derives each value
from its label **under a session nonce the server generated at startup**, which is what lets an
observed pair be checked instead of believed. That matters because
`<option value="Asian">Prefer not to answer</option>` is a page a form could serve: not being
able to read a value is not the same as the value being safe.

The nonce is also why a loopback address grants nothing on its own. Any local process can
listen on `127.0.0.1` and compute a published hash, so trust comes from a `replay_surfaces`
record Jobloom wrote when it started this renderer — bound to the exact origin, carrying a
digest over the vendored fixture bytes, the renderer version and the bytes of every page
served, expiring, and revoked when the server stops. Two live records for one origin fail
closed rather than resolving to the most recent, because two processes claiming one origin is
not something this can adjudicate.

The nonce is stored in plaintext in the private database. That is accepted for a local replay
whose pages carry no real data, on the terms that it stays inside the protected store — a test
asserts it reaches no event, package or archive — and it is **not** a key scheme for a future
production adapter. On any other surface an approved adapter mapping with a fixed
hash and version would be required, and none exists, so the control is the user's.

The final control is a real submit that posts to a loopback counting endpoint. An earlier
version was an inert button incrementing a `window` variable the server never read, which
reported zero whether or not anything had been activated: an oracle that could not fail is not
an oracle.
